cues.text: Section two: big-data architecture and platforms.
Let us begin with the overall picture, which the source gives as a diagram.
Read it from the top.
At the top we have sensors, web traffic and applications.
These are the origins of the data.
From there, data flows downward into Kafka ingestion.
Kafka then feeds a stream processor, and the stream processor sends its results to alerts and to an operational store.
So the fast path is: source, Kafka, stream processor, then alerts or an operational store.
Beneath Kafka, there is a second path going down into a raw data lake.
Notice that the stream processor also sends data downward.
Both the raw data lake and the stream processor feed into curated datasets.
From curated datasets, the data moves on to a warehouse and to business intelligence, or BI, tools.
So the slower path is: raw data lake, curated datasets, then warehouse and BI.
Finally, the diagram shows one more element running down the side, across all the layers: governance, catalog, quality and security.
This tells us these four concerns are not a single stage.
They apply across every layer of the architecture.
Now let us look at the technologies, starting with Apache Kafka.
Kafka is a distributed event log and streaming platform.
Producers publish records to topics, and each topic is divided into partitions.
Brokers are the servers that store the records, and consumers read them using offsets, which are positions in the log.
Consumers can be organised into consumer groups, and the members of a group share the partitions between them.
One important rule: ordering is guaranteed within a partition, but not globally across the whole topic.
Replication improves resilience, so the loss of a broker need not mean the loss of data.
Retention permits replay, meaning that records are kept for a period and consumers can read them again.
A caution from the source: Kafka is not itself a conventional analytical warehouse.
Consumers and processors are the ones that perform business transformations.
Another caution concerns delivery.

At-least-once processing can repeat messages, so you should use idempotency, which means that handling the same message twice has the same effect as handling it once, along with appropriate transaction semantics.
And the source qualifies exactly-once guarantees: they depend on the end-to-end architecture, not on Kafka alone.
Next, Hadoop.
Hadoop includes three parts.
HDFS is the distributed file storage.
YARN is for resource management.
MapReduce is for batch computation.
HDFS stores files in replicated blocks.
The NameNode manages the metadata, and the DataNodes store the blocks themselves.
MapReduce works in three steps.
Map transforms records into intermediate key and value pairs.
Shuffle groups those pairs by key.
Reduce aggregates each group.
The source's example is word count.
Map each word to the pair word and one.
Then group identical words together.
Then sum the counts for each word.
So if the word "data" appears three times, the shuffle gathers three pairs for "data", and reduce adds them to give three.
Hadoop supports large sequential operations well, but it is not ideal for tiny, low-latency point queries.
Now Spark.
Spark provides distributed computation using DAG execution, that is, a directed acyclic graph of steps, and it offers in-memory reuse when that is suitable.
It supports SQL, streaming and machine learning.
It can read from HDFS or from object storage.
But remember: Spark is not a durable database by itself.
Two more tools.
Hive provides SQL-oriented analytics over data lake storage.
HBase provides wide-column access on a distributed foundation.
And the source's closing point is that Kafka, Spark and Hadoop can complement one another rather than replace each other.
Now the worked ingestion sizing example.
We have 10,000 wearables.
Each sends one event of 200 bytes every five seconds.
First, the event rate: 10,000 divided by 5 gives 2,000 events per second.
Next, the raw payload.
2,000 events per second, each of 200 bytes, gives 400,000 bytes per second.
Over a day, that comes to 34.56 gigabytes, using decimal units.
Over seven days, that is approximately 241.92 gigabytes.
If we keep three replicated copies, the total is approximately 725.76 gigabytes.
The source stresses that this is before compression and metadata.
So the figure is only a starting point.
In real capacity planning you must also include headers, indexes, retry traffic and peak load.
Finally, a design lesson.
A batch warehouse query is not the right first destination for emergency alerts.
Stream processing can evaluate thresholds promptly.
That is exactly why the architecture sends data through the stream processor to alerts, rather than waiting for the warehouse.
